background.definition: The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) occurs when the level of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) remains elevated despite euvolemia and hyponatremia. It is a diagnosis of exclusion when the elevated ADH levels are not caused by excessive emotional stress, pain, diuretic use, or other drugs that stimulate ADH secretion. Patients with SIADH must have normal heart, liver, kidney, adrenal, and thyroid function.

list.listitem: Mild hyponatremia occurs in up to 15% to 22% of hospitalized patients; moderate to severe hyponatremia with sodium levels less than 130 mEq/L is estimated to be present in 1% to 4% of hospitalized patients.
The majority of cases of euvolemic hyponatremia are due to SIADH.
Infectious causes: pneumonia, empyema, HIV, intracranial abscess, meningitis, encephalitis, tuberculosis, and aspergillosis.
Iatrogenic secondary to use of hypotonic fluids.
Medications that stimulate ADH release: nicotine, phenothiazines, and tricyclic antidepressants.
Medications that potentiate ADH: desmopressin, oxytocin, and prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors.

Medications that have unknown or mixed mechanisms of action: angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, carbamazepine, chlorpropamide, ecstasy (3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine), selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, antipsychotics, duloxetine, cyclophosphamide, omeprazole, and vincristine.
Pulmonary and mediastinal tumors: bronchogenic carcinoma, mesothelioma, and thymomas.
Other pulmonary causes: respiratory failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and ventilator use.
Other tumors: lymphoma, uterine, duodenal, pancreatic, prostate, ureteral, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

Neurological conditions: tumors, hydrocephalus, atrophy, intracranial hemorrhage, neurotrauma, Guillain-Barre syndrome, stroke, spinal surgery, or spinal lesions. Patients undergoing care for traumatic brain surgery, aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, neurosurgery and ischemic stroke are at risk for SIADH and their sodium should be carefully monitored.
Idiopathic.
SIADH may be caused by many underlying medical conditions, all leading to a common pathway of elevated ADH despite normal plasma volume and hyponatremia.

Excessive ADH bonds to the ADH (vasopressin receptors) in the distal convoluted tubules and collecting ducts of the kidney. The activation of the receptor eventually leads to increased aquaporins in the membrane, allowing an increase in the influx of free water and small amounts of certain solutes to be reabsorbed by the kidney.
Persistent influx of water leads to continuing hyposmolality and hyponatremia.

Although most patients with syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) are asymptomatic, rapid changes in sodium concentration can cause mental status changes, convulsions, headaches, nausea, and vomiting. B
If a patient with hyponatremia is euvolemic, order serum chemistry, serum osmolality, and urine studies including osmolality and electrolytes. C
If a patient presents with a serum sodium level of less than 135 mEq/L, serum osmolality less than 275 mOsm/kg, and euvolemia consider SIADH as a possible diagnosis. C

SIADH is likely if euvolemic hypotonic hyponatremia is accompanied by urine osmolality greater than 100 mOsm/kg and urine sodium excretion greater than 30 mmol/L and can not be explained by any other disease process. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Obtaining a medication history can rule out medications as the cause of hyponatremia.
Primary or secondary adrenal insufficiency can be evaluated with a random cortisol level.
Patients tend to present with symptoms of heart failure, abnormal echocardiogram, elevated BNP, or edema.
Patients may present with hypoalbuminemia, edema, ascites, or abnormal liver function tests.
ADH can be suppressed at some level of osmolality, with decreased ADH at a plasma osmolality below a certain setpoint.

list.listitem: Diagnostic criteria are based on work done by Bartter and Schwartz in 1967 and reviewed by an expert panel of endocrinologists in 2007.
Key diagnostic criteria include hyponatremia with a serum sodium level of less than 135 mEq/L and serum osmolality less than 275 mOsm/kg H2O.
Clinical euvolemia must be present without evidence of hypovolemia or edema.
Urine osmolality should be greater than 100 mOsm/kg, or greater than maximally dilute urine.
As SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion, there must be normal heart, liver, kidney, adrenal, and thyroid function.
Finally, no other causes including medications or other medical conditions causing hyposmolality are present.
If SIADH is suspected, a detailed history and physical examination should be performed to determine the patient's volume status and to rule out other causes of their condition.
Most patients with SIADH and hyponatremia are asymptomatic, with symptoms occurring when the serum sodium falls below 125 mEq/L or if there is a rapid drop in sodium.

If patients have symptoms, neurologic conditions predominate with complaints of headache, lethargy, restlessness, confusion, coma, or respiratory distress. Other somatic symptoms may include muscle cramps, nausea, and vomiting.
If a rapid fall in the sodium level occurs, the patient may have more severe symptoms including muscular twitches, irritability, or convulsions.
If SIADH is considered, order serum electrolytes and osmolality, urine osmolality, and urine electrolytes.

As SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion, other tests should be considered to ensure the patient has normal thyroid, liver, cardiac, kidney, and adrenal function. These may include thyroid stimulating hormone, T3, T4, liver function tests, albumin, brain natriuretic peptide, creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, and random cortisol.

Based on the diagnostic criteria of Bartter and Schwartz, the patient must be euvolemic and have a serum sodium level of less than 135 mEq/L, serum osmolality less than 275 mOsm/L, urine osmolality greater than 100 mOsm/L, and urine sodium greater than 30 mmol/L without other causes of hyponatremia.
One study suggests that the optimal cutoff for diagnosis of SIADH vs hypovolemic hyponatremia is 50 mEq/L (89% sensitive, 69% specific, area under ROC curve 0.89.
In post-operative patients being given normal saline, SIADH can be masked, with normal sodium levels. In these patients, weight gain is greater as are ADH levels 24 to 48 hours post-operatively.
See in Hyponatremia chapter for a suggested approach to the evaluation of the patient with low serum sodium.
See for a suggested approach to acute hyponatremia due to SIADH, and for a suggested approach to chronic hyponatremia due to SIADH.
Treat the underlying condition or stop the medication that is causing syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH), if possible. C
Fluid restriction is first-line therapy. B
Hypertonic 3% saline is the recommended treatment for symptomatic hyponatremia; loop diuretics are effective for decreasing edema caused by treatment with 3% saline. B
Demeclocycline, lithium, and urea can be used for mild cases of chronic asymptomatic hyponatremia. B
Vaptans (tolvaptan, conivaptan, satavaptan) have been shown to safely normalize sodium levels in patients with SIADH. B
Frequent monitoring of serum sodium is recommended during the active phase of treatment to reduce the risk of rapid changes in the sodium level and serious injury to patients. C

Treat the underlying condition that is causing SIADH, including discontinuation of any causative medications. A consensus guideline provides a suggested pathway for patients with SIADH due to psychiatric medications.

Hypertonic (3%) saline is the treatment of choice for symptomatic hyponatremia. Loop diuretics (furosemide, torsemide, ethacrynic acid, bumetanide) may be used as needed for volume overload from treatment using 3% normal saline. To determine the infusion rate, multiply the patient weight in kilograms by the desired rate of increase in serum sodium. For example, in an 80 kg patient, infusing 3% NaCl at 40 mL per hour will increase the serum sodium by approximately 0.5 mEq/L per hour, and a rate of 80 mL per hour will increase it by 1 mEq/L per hour. See below for recommended rates of increase.

For acute symptomatic hyponatremia less than 48 hours in duration, the goal is to have a change of sodium of 1 mEq/L to 2 mEq/L per hour until sodium levels have reached a level greater than 120 mEql/L, the patient is asymptomatic, or the change of sodium is greater than 18 mEq/L in a 24-hour period. The sodium level must be checked every 2 to 4 hours to decrease the risk of too rapid a change in sodium levels.

For chronic symptomatic hyponatremia, the rate of change should be slower. An increase of serum sodium of 0.5 mEq/L per hour, or 12 mEq/L the first day, with a total of no more than 18 mEq/L for the first 2 days, is recommended.

Recent research indicates that a new medication class—vasopressin V2-receptor antagonists (vaptans)—shows promise. Conivaptan (Vaprisol) 20 mg to 40 mg IV daily for a maximum of 4 days is the only vaptan available in the United States that is FDA-approved for acute symptomatic euvolemic hyponatremia. Other oral versions have shown promise and are available in countries outside the United States, including tolvaptan in 15, 30, and 60 mg doses.

A systematic review of observational studies (n=18, 495 patients) found that lower initial doses of tolvaptan may be effective. A dose of 7.5 mg increased sodium by a mean of 7.8 mmol/L within 24 hours. The mean increase was 7.1 mg for a 3.75 mg dose. Randomized trials are needed.
Most studies have shown them effective to improve sodium levels, but no patient-oriented outcome evidence is available at this time.
An economic analysis concluded that use of vaptans in hospitalized patients with SIADH has the potential to reduce length of stay and ICU admissions and be cost-effective.

Other medications may be used for chronic asymptomatic hyponatremia. These include lithium, which impairs AVP/ADH at the renal tubules; oral demeclocycline 300 mg 2 to 4 times a day, which generates a nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; and oral urea at 30 g per day to decrease sodium excretion. In conjunction with free water restriction, these treatments tend to decrease sodium levels slowly, so changes may not be seen for up to 3 days after initiation of treatment.Regarding demeclocycline, a systematic review found relatively little research evidence regarding its efficacy or the optimal dose.
Older treatments for hyponatremia (phenylhydantoin, opiates, and alcohol) are no longer recommended because of their side effects and unpredictability.
Treat the underlying surgical condition, if one exists.
Patients undergoing care for traumatic brain surgery, aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, neurosurgery and ischemic stroke are at risk for SIADH and their sodium should be carefully monitored.

First line therapy is fluid restriction: recommend water restriction of no more than 750 to 1000 mL daily. Alternatively, restrict free water to the 24-hour urine volume minus 500 mL. Since total body sodium may be low, no sodium restriction is needed. However, water restriction may be challenging given the extreme thirst often present.
Fluid restriction can be used to treat the asymptomatic hyponatremia associated with venlafaxine.

A study randomized 46 patients with chronic asymptomatic SIADH (median Na+ 127 mmol/L) to fluid restriction of 1 liter/day or no therapy for 1 moonth. After 30 days 61% in the fluid restriction group had achieved a serum sodium of at least 130 mmol/L, compared with 39% in the comparison group (p = 0.24).

A Thai study randomized 91 patients with SIADH to fluid restriction alone, fluid restriction + furosemide 20 to 40 mg/day, or fluid restriction + furosemide + 3 gm oral sodium daily. All interventions worked equally well, increasing the serum sodium by approximately 5 mmol/L over 28 days, but acute kidney injury and hypokalemia were more common in the groups receiving furosemide.
Increased morbidity and all-cause mortality has been shown for all patients with hyponatremia regardless of treatment. B
There is a very high risk of death or neurologic sequelae with overly rapid or delayed correction of hyponatremia. B
If untreated, a persistent decrease in osmolality and possible worsening of hyponatremia can lead to serious neurologic outcomes or death.
Up to 45% of patients with hyponatremia also have abnormalities of other electrolytes, including hypophosphatemia, hyper/hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypo/hypercalcemia.
In 7 patients with traumatic brain injury who had SIADH after injury, all regained normal sodium and resolution of SIADH within 6 to 12 months without specific therapy.
Different published studies have shown various rates of morbidity and mortality.
The rate of death or major morbidity can be up to 80% for severe hyponatremia, defined as a serum sodium of less than 130 mEq/L with neurologic symptoms.
Other studies have shown a much lower rate of death (8%) with severe symptomatic hyponatremia with sodium levels of less than 105 mEq/L.

More rapid changes to the serum sodium level in chronic hyponatremia increases the risk of central pontine myelinolysis, neurologic sequelae, or death due to rapid swelling of the brain. These complications may not be evident until 4 to 6 days after the sodium has been corrected.

Frequent monitoring of serum sodium is recommended during the active phase of treatment to reduce the risk of rapid changes in sodium level and serious injury to patients. During initial therapy with 3% saline, serum sodium level must be monitored at least every 2 to 4 hours.
Once the 3% saline has been discontinued, the serum sodium should be measured every 4 to 8 hours until the sodium level has stabilized.

algorithm.title: Acute Hyponatremia Due to SIADH: Treatment.

cell.label: Fluid restriction < 1000 ml/day, 3% normal saline at 1-2 mL/kg/hr Alternative: conivaptan 20-40 mg IV divided BID for a maximum of 4 days or tolvaptan 15-30 mg/day.
Reassess volume status, neurological status, and electrolytes every 2-4 hours. If edema, furosemide 20-40 mg IV every 2 hours PRN (maximum dose of 0.4 mg/kg/hr).
Neurologic symptoms present, [Na] ≤120 mEq/L, or change in [Na] ≤18 mEq/L in 24 hours.
Adjust rate to keep change of [Na] at 1-2 mEq/L/hr or <18 mEq/L in 24 hours.
Discontinue 3% NS and continue to follow [Na] every 4-8 hours until stable levels are reached.
Treat underlying cause; monitor [Na] and neurologic symptoms daily.

footnotes.footnote: †Estimating the initial rate of 3% NS in mL/hr by multiplying the patient's weight in kg X the desired rate of change in mL/kg/hr.
Data from Verbalis JG, Goldsmith SR, Greenberg A, Schrier RW, Sterns RH. Hyponatremia Treatment Guidelines 2007: Expert Panel Recommendations. Am J Med 2007;120:S1–S21.

algorithm.title: Chronic Hyponatremia Due to SIADH: Treatment.

cell.label: Reassess volume status, neurological status, and electrolytes every 2-4 hours. If edema, furosemide 20-40 mg IV every 2 hours PRN. Maximum dose = 0.4 mg/kg/hr.
Neurologic symptoms present, [Na] ≤120 mEq/L, or change in [Na] ≤12 mEq/L in 24 hours?
Adjust rate to keep change of [Na] <0.5 mEql/L/hr or <12mEq/L in 24 hours.
Discontinue 3% NS and continue to follow [Na] every 4-8 hours until stable levels are reached.
Restrict water to daily urine minus 500 mL/day. No NaCl restriction.
Recheck daily serum [Na] and osmolality. Improved at 3 days?
If no alternative diagnosis suspected, consider second-line treatments: (1) demeclocyclinje 600-1200 mg/day in divided doses; (2) urea 30 g once daily; or (3) lithium.
